solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Best to snub leader with lively goal for education

indicators.note: to snub the leader is to cut the front runner, so the opening letter is dropped

blocks.note: the best are the elite; without its first letter
racy writing is lively and spirited

explanation.surface: Advice for a school: forget pleasing the top brass and set an energetic target for learning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Best' as a noun means the cream, the chosen few; snubbing their leader removes the opening letter. 'Goal for education' is the definition, not part of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Being able to read and write is the basic aim of any schooling system.

clue.text: Girl wanting second vehicle for sailor from the east

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so something is taken away

blocks.note: a lass is a girl; the S for second is removed
S is the abbreviation for second, the letter taken out
a car is a vehicle

explanation.surface: A girl in need of a second car, perhaps after a family gets bigger.
explanation.walkthrough: LASS minus one S (second) gives LAS, then CAR. 'For' links wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Lascar is the historical term for a seaman from India or Southeast Asia serving on European ships.

clue.text: I comment when leaving stores for headgear

indicators.note: whatever stores something keeps it inside, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: taken as written
ta-ra is a northern English way of saying goodbye

explanation.surface: Someone about to walk out with the shop's hat collection.
explanation.walkthrough: TA-RA, a cheery British goodbye (like 'bye-bye'), holds I: T(I)ARA.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiara is a jewelled ornamental band worn on the head, a type of headwear.

clue.text: Most Croesus-like king, one hoarder of treasure?

blocks.note: R for rex, Latin for king
the Roman numeral for one
a treasure chest holds a hoard

explanation.surface: A fabulously wealthy monarch who is also a miser sitting on his gold.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that a chest 'hoards' treasure only figuratively.
explanation.definitionFit: Croesus, the ancient Lydian king, was proverbially wealthy, so being most like him means having the greatest fortune.

clue.text: Birds caught with trouble are located among larks

indicators.note: to be among things is to sit in the midst of them, so one part goes inside the other

blocks.note: C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
to ail is to trouble or afflict
things that lie somewhere are located there
larks and capers are both bits of mischievous fun

explanation.surface: Birdwatchers spot some other species caught up in trouble among a flock of larks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Larks' looks like more birds but means pranks, and it is split open to take the three short pieces inside, just before its final S.
explanation.definitionFit: Capercaillies are large woodland grouse of Scotland and northern Europe, so they are a kind of game bird.

clue.text: Group participating in Monopoly react badly, beginning to lose

indicators.note: done badly means done wrongly, so the letters come out in a muddled order
the beginning of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged
the opening letter of lose

explanation.surface: Board-game players react badly when they start to lose at Monopoly.
explanation.walkthrough: Monopoly looks like the board game; here it is the economic sense, a market controlled by one group.
explanation.definitionFit: A cartel is an association of firms that fixes prices together, which is how a monopoly can be shared.

clue.text: V sign America’s leader deployed at borders

indicators.note: a leader is at the front, so only the opening letter is used
troops deployed are spread out into new positions, so letters are rearranged
a border runs round the edge, so these two letters go on the outside

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
the opening letter of America
taken as written, split around the rest

explanation.surface: Someone describes the rude two-finger gesture spreading across America's borders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'V sign' reads as one gesture, but V stands alone as the definition. SIGN plus A becomes GAINS, framed by A and T.
explanation.definitionFit: V is short for versus, used in sports fixtures and court cases to mean opposed to or competing with.

clue.text: Ambassador’s absorbed by sign one will offer alternative terms

indicators.note: what is absorbed is taken in, so one piece ends up inside another

blocks.note: HE, His Excellency, is how an ambassador is styled; plus the S of 's
Taurus is a sign of the zodiac

explanation.surface: A diplomat engrossed in a signal from someone proposing different conditions for a deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Alternative terms' sounds like negotiation; it means synonyms. His Excellency (HE) is the formal title of an ambassador.
explanation.definitionFit: A thesaurus is a reference book listing synonyms, other words a writer might use instead.

clue.text: Influencer is TikTok’s first to follow Chuck Berry’s cover

indicators.note: first points to the opening letter of the word before it
a cover wraps the outside, so only the two outer letters are kept
to follow is to come after, fixing which part goes at the end

blocks.note: to lob is to chuck or throw
the outside letters of Berry
taken as written
the opening letter of TikTok

explanation.surface: A social media star covers a Chuck Berry song on TikTok.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Influencer' and 'Chuck Berry' both look like people; one is a definition, the other a verb and a word.
explanation.definitionFit: A lobbyist is paid to sway politicians on behalf of a cause, the older sense of an influencer.

clue.text: Whiskery swimmers ignoring large headlands, or views from them?

indicators.note: to ignore something is to leave it out, so a letter is dropped

blocks.note: seals have whiskers; the L for large is removed
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large, the letter taken out
a cape is a headland jutting into the sea

explanation.surface: Seals swimming past big promontories, or perhaps the vistas you would see from those promontories.
explanation.walkthrough: SEALS without L leaves SEAS. 'Them' points back to the headlands: from a cape you look out over the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A seascape is a view or picture of the sea, just what a clifftop headland offers.

clue.text: Need cash when tailored clothes shrink — it’s a nasty feeling

indicators.note: tailored cloth is cut and reshaped, so these letters are refashioned
to clothe something is to wrap it up, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged
a shrink is a psychiatrist, and Sigmund Freud is the most famous

explanation.surface: Being short of money when your made-to-measure clothes have shrunk in the wash: a horrible feeling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clothes' looks like a noun for garments but is a verb: the rearranged letters wrap round the psychiatrist, just before the final E.
explanation.definitionFit: Schadenfreude is the German-borrowed word for pleasure taken in another's misfortune, an unkind and spiteful emotion.

clue.text: Very cool beer drained and knocked back is bitter

indicators.note: a drained vessel is emptied of its contents, leaving only its shell
knocked back means sent backwards, so the order turns round

blocks.note: ace is slang for excellent, very cool
the outside letters of beer, its middle emptied

explanation.surface: A drinker downs a chilled pint and pronounces it bitter, as in the English ale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocked back' suggests drinking the beer; here it turns the two leftover letters round. Bitter is a British style of ale, but here it is an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Acerb is a rare word for sour or harsh in taste or tone, the same root as acerbic.

clue.text: Perhaps old Dutch gold rings right for dabbler

indicators.note: a ring surrounds whatever sits in it, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: 'my old Dutch' is Cockney slang for a wife, one kind of mate or partner
Au is the chemical symbol for gold
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: An antique Dutch gold ring, set aside for a hobbyist collector.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old Dutch' looks like a historical reference to Holland; in Cockney slang it is a man's wife, hence 'perhaps' for a mate.
explanation.definitionFit: An amateur does something for pleasure rather than pay, often without deep skill, like a dabbler.

clue.text: Country’s empty housing area

indicators.note: a house holds its occupants inside, so one piece contains the other

blocks.note: an empty stomach is a hungry one
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: A nation with unoccupied homes across a whole region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Housing area' reads as a residential estate, but 'housing' is the container verb. The 's is 'is', linking definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Hungary is a landlocked nation in central Europe with Budapest as its capital.

clue.text: Alexander not finishing small pastries after suit bursts

indicators.note: not finishing means stopping short, so the final letter is lost
after means coming later, so what follows is placed behind

blocks.note: to suit is to fit
Sandy is a pet form of Alexander; the last letter goes
S is the abbreviation for small
tarts are pastries

explanation.surface: Alexander leaves his little cakes half-eaten after bursting out of his suit.
explanation.walkthrough: Sandy is a Scottish short form of Alexander. 'Bursts' seems to describe the suit but is the definition, a plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Proceeding by fits and starts means working in irregular spurts rather than steadily, so short bursts of activity.

clue.text: Cracking shooting jackets South American returned

indicators.note: a jacket is worn around the body, so one piece wraps the other
returned means sent back, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: shooting a gun is firing it
S is the abbreviation for South
US, as in a US citizen, stands for American

explanation.surface: A spectacular shoot of jackets by a South American photographer back home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'South American' looks like one phrase for a continent but splits into S and US, and only the second part is turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: To fissure is to split or open up in narrow cracks, so fissuring is splitting apart.

clue.text: The person setting up stage show initially stresses

indicators.note: in a down clue, set up means raised from bottom to top, so the order flips
initially points to the opening letter of the word before it

blocks.note: the person setting the puzzle refers to themself as me
a stage in a process is a phase
the opening letter of show

explanation.surface: A theatre producer is anxious about mounting the first stage show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The person setting' is the crossword setter, who refers to themselves as ME. 'Stresses' is a plural noun here, not a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Emphases are points of special weight or importance, as stresses in speech or argument.

clue.text: Divers with no clue, aimless at sea

indicators.note: at sea means confused and disoriented, so these letters are jumbled

blocks.note: letters to be rearranged
letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Scuba divers have lost their bearings and drift aimlessly in the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Divers' looks like people who swim underwater; here it is an old adjective, pronounced DYE-verse, meaning several different.
explanation.definitionFit: Divers, an archaic word for sundry or of various kinds, means a mixed assortment, which miscellaneous also describes.

clue.text: Glaring, upset detective overwhelmed by incident

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means tipped up, so the letters read bottom to top
to be overwhelmed is to be engulfed, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: DI is a Detective Inspector
an incident is an event

explanation.surface: A detective, angry and upset, is swamped by a case that is going badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Glaring' looks like the detective's angry stare, but it is the definition in the sense of obvious.
explanation.definitionFit: A glaring error is plainly obvious to everyone, just as something evident is clearly seen.

clue.text: Wham too forcefully finished popular song?

blocks.note: something finished is over
a popular song is a hit

explanation.surface: Did the pop duo Wham! wrap up their chart-topping single?
explanation.walkthrough: The capital W and question mark suggest Wham!, the 1980s band; here 'wham' is a plain verb meaning to strike.
explanation.definitionFit: To overhit a ball is to strike it harder than needed, in tennis or golf for example.

clue.text: Free book prefaces with a line of The Woman in White?

indicators.note: a preface comes before the main text, so this piece is put in front

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for book
to free is to rid
taken as written
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A free book featuring an opening line from Wilkie Collins's Victorian novel The Woman in White.
explanation.walkthrough: The Woman in White looks like the novel's title; with the question mark it becomes a bride in her white gown.
explanation.definitionFit: Bridal means relating to a bride, and a bride traditionally wears a white wedding dress.

clue.text: Chap unlikely to stay confined in hotel in France agreed to stifle noise

indicators.note: to stifle is to smother, so one piece is wrapped inside the other

blocks.note: H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet
oui is French for yes
a din is a loud noise

explanation.surface: A guest who will not stay in his room at a French hotel, promising to keep the noise down.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'in' joins definition to wordplay; the second belongs to 'in France', which makes the yes French.
explanation.definitionFit: Harry Houdini was the famous escapologist, the performer no chains, locks or cells could hold.

clue.text: Someone who lets engaging European enlist again

indicators.note: gears engaging mesh together, taking something in, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: a renter can be a landlord who lets property out
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A landlord takes on a European tenant who is signing up for another stint.
explanation.walkthrough: A renter is usually the tenant, but it can also mean the one who rents a property out, which is what 'lets' points to.
explanation.definitionFit: To re-enter a contest or service is to sign up for it once more, joining up a second time.

clue.text: Ex-president saving man I’m not sure is more faithful

indicators.note: saving in the sense of except means leaving out, so these letters go

blocks.note: Harry Truman was a US president; take away the letters for a man
the letters removed from the president's name
er is the hesitant sound of uncertainty

explanation.surface: A doubtful voter wonders whether a former president rescuing someone shows more loyalty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saving' seems to mean rescuing, but it means except: TRUMAN minus MAN.
explanation.definitionFit: True means loyal or steadfast, so truer is the comparative, more loyal.

clue.text: Maybe remove dust from behind Saint Nick

indicators.note: behind means at the back, so this piece is placed second

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for Saint
wiping is one way to remove dust

explanation.surface: Someone dusting behind a statue of St Nicholas, Santa Claus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saint Nick' reads as Santa; split, Saint becomes the abbreviation and Nick is the verb meaning steal, British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: To nick and to swipe are both informal verbs for stealing, especially a small item.

clue.text: Abundant amusement in vacant shed Kitty used for nefarious purposes

indicators.note: a vacant place has nothing inside, so only the outer letters remain
in places one piece inside another

blocks.note: lush growth is abundant
fun is amusement
the outside letters of shed

explanation.surface: A cat finds lots of fun in an empty garden shed, put to sinister use.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kitty' looks like the cat in the shed; it is the definition, a pool of money.
explanation.definitionFit: A kitty is a shared pot of money, and a slush fund is one kept for bribes or other illicit spending.

clue.text: Picks out large pants, saving time

indicators.note: to save something is to keep it safe within, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: big heavy breaths, as when pants are deep, are sighs
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Someone selects outsize underpants to save time dressing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pants' is British for underwear, which the surface wants, but here it is the plural of a breath, and large ones are sighs.
explanation.definitionFit: To sight something is to spot or catch view of it, as picking out a ship on the horizon.

clue.text: Muscle shown by East End bully punching friend

indicators.note: Cockneys of London's East End famously drop their H sounds
a punch drives into something, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: to hector is to bully, and the opening H is dropped
a pal is a friend

explanation.surface: A Cockney thug showing off his muscles as he punches his mate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bully' looks like a noun for the thug but is a verb here. The East End is the traditional Cockney area of London.
explanation.definitionFit: The pectorals are the large chest muscles, and a pectoral is any one of them.
